hints: Focus on the single carbon atom that carries the OH group, not on the whole molecule or the number of OH groups.
Count how many other carbon atoms are directly joined to that C-OH carbon: one means primary, two means secondary, three means tertiary.
Test each row in order and look for the row where the C-OH carbon goes from 1 to 2 to 3 attached carbons across the columns.
walkthrough:
**Recall the rule for classification**

Alcohols are classified by the environment of the carbon bonded to OH. It is a lovely simple counting rule.

$\text{primary: C-OH joined to 1 other C, secondary: joined to 2 other Cs, tertiary: joined to 3 other Cs}$

**Check what row D shows**

Primary column is $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH}_2\text{-OH}$. The $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ carbon is joined to only 1 other carbon, so primary.

Secondary column is $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH(OH)-CH}_3$. The $\text{CHOH}$ carbon is joined to 2 other carbons, so secondary.

**Confirm the tertiary structure**

Tertiary column is $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C-OH}$. The central $\text{C-OH}$ carbon is joined to 3 methyl carbons and no hydrogens, so tertiary.

That gives primary, secondary, tertiary in order, so this row is fully correct.

options.A: First two are correct: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is primary and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$ contains a secondary alcohol. The third structure $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$ has only $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ (primary) and $\text{CHOH}$ (secondary) carbons, with no carbon joined to three other carbons, so it is not tertiary.
options.B: The primary column $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{OH}$ is indeed primary. But the labels are then swapped: the middle structure $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C-OH}$ has C-OH joined to 3 carbons so it is tertiary, not secondary, and the right structure with $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is primary, not tertiary.
options.C: The left structure is primary ($\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$). However the middle and right structures both contain only $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ groups. A $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ carbon is always joined to only one other carbon, so both are primary alcohols, not secondary and tertiary. Extra OH groups do not change the class.
options.D: Perfect match: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ has C-OH joined to 1 C (primary), $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ has C-OH joined to 2 Cs (secondary), and $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C-OH}$ has C-OH joined to 3 Cs (tertiary). This is ethanol, propan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
